summary: IODEF version 2, defined in RFC 7970, is a data format for sharing information about computer security incidents. Because it has many options, this document gives guidance on how to use them in practice so that different teams produce and understand each other's reports.

eli5.summary: It is a handbook for filling out an incident report form, so everyone fills in the same blanks the same way.

subtitle: A handbook for implementing incident sharing with IODEF v2.

tldr.problem: IODEF v2 defines a comprehensive format for sharing security incident information, but its many options make it hard for organizations to implement consistently.
tldr.mechanism: This document provides practical guidance on which IODEF classes and fields to implement for common incident types like DDoS, malware, and phishing, and explains how to use IODEF's extensibility features.
tldr.outcome: Organizations using IODEF can build compatible tools and exchange incident information more reliably, making coordinated threat response faster and easier.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 7970 defines IODEF v2 (Incident Object Description Exchange Format version 2), a comprehensive XML-based data model for representing and exchanging information about computer security incidents. CSIRTs (Computer Security Incident Response Teams) and vendors use IODEF to share details about attacks, breaches, malware, and other security events.

The IODEF schema includes a wealth of classes and optional fields designed to cover all possible incident types. This flexibility is powerful but creates a practical problem: implementers struggle to decide which classes to use, and different vendors implement different subsets, making interoperability difficult. This document provides guidelines to make IODEF adoption easier.
sections.eli5: IODEF is a standardized way to write down details about a security attack. This RFC teaches you what to write down and how, so everyone understands the same things the same way.

sections.title: IODEF Structure and Key Concepts
sections.content:
A minimal IODEF document requires an Incident class with a purpose attribute, a GenerationTime (when the incident was created), an IncidentID (a unique name), and at least one Contact element identifying who submitted the report.

The schema distinguishes between IndicatorData (threat indicators that were observed or prevented) and EventData (security events that actually took place). Supporting classes like Discovery, Assessment, and Method add context only when describing events. Other important classes include Flow (for network traffic details in DDoS attacks) and FileData (for malware samples).

Implementers should not try to support the entire schema. Instead, they should identify their use cases and implement only the classes needed for them. Parsing classes you do not use is waste.
sections.eli5: An IODEF report has a minimum: who reported it, when, and a name. Then you add details depending on what happened: network flows for DDoS, file information for malware, email details for phishing.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
IODEF supports external references via the Reference class, which can cite CVEs, IDS alerts, vulnerability databases, or attack frameworks using the enumeration reference format defined in RFC 7495. Implementers should only support the external enumerations relevant to their use cases (CVE, CVRF, OVAL, etc.).

The schema is extensible: attributes with enumerated values can be extended with an ext-* prefix, and new classes can be added via AdditionalData and RecordItem elements. For complex data, IODEF can import external schemas (like CVRF or OVAL) using the framework in RFC 7203. Implementers should prefer existing standards over creating custom extensions.

When describing indicators with logic (for example, matching if any one of three C2 servers is detected), the IndicatorExpression class allows Boolean operators (AND, OR) to group observables and other indicators.

Access control is managed via the restriction attribute, which signals the disclosure level (for example, a CSIRT might mark sensitive details as restricted). The Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) protocol, defined in RFC 6545, can enforce these restrictions when transporting IODEF documents over TLS.
sections.eli5: You can add your own details to a report, link it to CVE numbers, use Yes/No logic to describe what triggered the alert, and mark parts as secret so only trusted partners see them.

sections.title: Real-World Use Cases
sections.content:
This document describes an interoperability exercise conducted in 2013 where vendors exchanged IODEF incident reports using RID over TLS. The exercise demonstrated five practical use cases:

Malware: A CSIRT detects malware on customer systems. IODEF describes the file hash, registry changes, and command-and-control server addresses. Sharing this with peers lets them identify infections in their networks and block the C2 traffic.

DDoS attacks: When a data center or ISP detects abnormal traffic saturation from a DDoS attack, it shares attack characteristics (source IP addresses, protocols, ports, HTTP user agents) with upstream networks using IODEF. Neighboring ISPs can then filter the traffic before it reaches the victim.

Spear phishing: A malicious email targeting specific individuals is reported to a corporate CSIRT. IODEF describes attachment metadata (file name, hash, size, malware family), target information (IP, domain, DNS lookups), email headers and timestamps, and confidence scores. Security teams share these indicators with partners to block similar campaigns.

Other use cases include ISPs notifying national CERTs of incidents, automated detection of malicious certificates for revocation, and bulk sharing of phishing emails across organizations.
sections.eli5: A company finds malware and shares the details in IODEF. Another company checks and finds the same malware in their network, so it blocks the bad connections. That teamwork protects everyone faster.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
This document does not introduce new security issues because it only provides guidance on RFC 7970. However, readers should review the Security Considerations in RFC 7970 itself.

IODEF documents can contain highly sensitive information: indicators used to detect ongoing attacks, attack infrastructure details, and compromised system information. The restriction attribute allows senders to signal how recipients should handle the data, but enforcement depends on operational measures (such as access control and encryption) implemented outside of IODEF.
sections.eli5: Incident reports are secret. Mark them carefully so only the right people see them, and use encrypted connections to send them.
